paragraphs: People often ask how individuals, who have no right to dispose of their own lives, can transfer to the Sovereign a right they do not possess. The difficulty of answering this question seems to me to lie in its being wrongly stated. Every man has a right to risk his own life in order to preserve it. Has anyone ever said that a man who throws himself out of a window to escape a fire is guilty of suicide? Has such a crime ever been charged against someone who dies in a storm because he knew of the danger when he went on board?

The social compact has as its end the preservation of the contracting parties. He who wills the end wills the means also, and the means must involve some risks, and even some losses. Anyone who wants to keep his own life at the expense of others should also be ready, when necessary, to give it up for their sake. Furthermore, the citizen is no longer the judge of the dangers to which the law requires him to expose himself. And when the prince says to him, “It is expedient for the State that you should die,” he ought to die. For it is only on that condition that he has been living in security up to now, and his life is no longer a mere bounty of nature, but a gift made conditionally by the State.

The death penalty inflicted on criminals may be looked at in much the same light. It is so that we may not fall victim to an assassin that we consent to die if we ourselves become assassins. In this compact, far from disposing of our own lives, we think only of securing them, and it is not to be assumed that any of the parties expects, at that moment, to get hanged.

Again, every wrongdoer who attacks social rights becomes, by his offense, a rebel and a traitor to his country. By violating its laws he ceases to be a member of it, and he even makes war on it. In such a case the preservation of the State is inconsistent with his own, and one or the other must perish. In putting the guilty to death, we kill not so much a citizen as an enemy. The trial and the judgment are the proofs that he has broken the social compact and is therefore no longer a member of the State. Since he recognized himself to be a member by living there, he must be removed from it, by exile as a violator of the compact, or by death as a public enemy. For such an enemy is not a moral person, but merely a man, and in such a case the right of war is to kill the vanquished.

But, it will be said, the condemnation of a criminal is a particular act. I admit it. But such condemnation is not a function of the Sovereign. It is a right the Sovereign can confer without being able to exercise it itself. All my ideas are consistent, but I cannot set them all out at once.

We may add that frequent punishments are always a sign of weakness or slackness on the part of the government. There is not a single wrongdoer who could not be made good for something. The State has no right to put anyone to death, even as an example, if it can leave him alive without danger.

The right of pardoning, or of exempting the guilty from a penalty imposed by the law and pronounced by the judge, belongs only to the authority that is superior to both judge and law, _i.e._ the Sovereign. Even its right in this matter is far from clear, and the occasions for using it are extremely rare. In a well-governed State there are few punishments, not because there are many pardons, but because there are few criminals. It is when a State is in decay that the multitude of crimes guarantees impunity. Under the Roman Republic, neither the Senate nor the Consuls ever attempted to pardon. Even the people never did, though it sometimes revoked its own decision. Frequent pardons mean that crime will soon have no need of them, and no one can fail to see where that leads. But I feel my heart protesting and holding back my pen. Let us leave these questions to the just man who has never offended and would himself never need pardon.
